questions.question: How does HashMap work internally in Java?
questions.title: HashMap Internals
questions.direct_answer: A **HashMap** stores entries in an **array of buckets**. On `put`, it computes the key's `hashCode()`, spreads it, and reduces it to a bucket index; collisions in a bucket form a **linked list** (a **red-black tree** past 8 entries since Java 8). When size exceeds **capacity x load factor (0.75)**, it **resizes** (doubles) and rehashes. `get` repeats the hashing to find the bucket, then uses `equals()` to find the exact key.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can explain buckets, hashing, collision handling, and resizing end to end
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Skipping the role of equals() in collision resolution, or forgetting treeification and load factor
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk the full put/get path: hash -> index -> bucket -> equals; mention treeify at 8 and resize at 0.75

sections.title: Buckets, Hashing, and Collisions
sections.content:
A **HashMap** stores **key-value pairs** so you can look a value up by its key. That is the part most beginners already half-know.

Under the hood it is an **array of buckets** (`Node<K,V>[] table`). When you call `put`, HashMap takes the key's `hashCode()`, applies a **spread** function (it mixes the high bits down so they influence the index), and reduces it to a **bucket index** with `hash & (capacity - 1)`.

When two keys land in the same bucket, that is a **collision**. The entries link together — first as a **linked list**, and since Java 8, once one bucket holds more than **8 entries**, that list converts to a **red-black tree** for `O(log n)` worst-case lookup.

The table also grows. Once the entry count passes **capacity x load factor** (default load factor **0.75**), HashMap **resizes** to double the capacity and **rehashes** every entry into the larger array.

A `get` repeats the same hashing to find the bucket, then walks it calling `equals()` to pick the exact key.

> **Key rule:** `hashCode()` gets you to the bucket; `equals()` finds the key inside it. Both must agree.

sections.title: HashMap Bucket Structure
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB K[key.hashCode] --> S[spread: mix high bits] S --> I[index = hash AND capacity-1] I --> T[bucket array] T --> B0[bucket 0] T --> B1[bucket 1: linked list] T --> B2[bucket 2: red-black tree
treeified > 8] B1 --> N1[node: key,value,next] N1 --> N2[node: key,value,next] R{size > cap * 0.75?} -->|yes| RZ[resize x2 + rehash] ```

sections.title: The put() Path
sections.content:
1. Compute `hashCode()` of the key, then **spread** it (mix high bits).
2. Reduce to an index: `hash & (capacity - 1)`.
3. Go to that bucket. If empty, place the node.
4. If occupied (**collision**), walk the list/tree; if a key **`equals()`** an existing one, **overwrite** the value; otherwise **append** the new node.
5. If the bucket passes 8 entries, **treeify** it.
6. If `size > capacity x 0.75`, **resize** (double) and rehash.

sections.title: Observing the Behavior
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting `equals()`.** `hashCode()` only narrows to a bucket; `equals()` picks the exact key inside it. Both are needed.
- **Skipping treeification.** Since Java 8 a bucket past 8 entries becomes a red-black tree, so the worst case is `O(log n)`, not `O(n)`.
- **Ignoring the load factor.** Resizing fires at `size > capacity x 0.75`, doubling and rehashing — an O(n) cost worth knowing.
- **Mutable keys.** If a key's hash-affecting field changes after insertion, its entry is lost in the wrong bucket.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Backed by an **array of buckets** (`Node<K,V>[] table`).
- Index = **spread(hashCode) & (capacity - 1)**.
- Collisions form a **linked list**, treeified to a **red-black tree** past 8 entries (Java 8+).
- **Resize** at `size > capacity x 0.75` (default load factor) — doubles and rehashes.
- `hashCode()` finds the **bucket**; `equals()` finds the **exact key**.
- Same key (by `equals`) on `put` **overwrites** the value.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Internally, a HashMap is an array of buckets. When you put a key-value pair, HashMap takes the key's hashCode, then applies a spreading function that mixes the high bits down so they actually influence the result, and reduces it to a bucket index using a bitwise and with capacity minus one. Then it goes to that bucket. If the bucket is empty, it just places the entry there. If something is already there — that's a collision — it walks the existing entries. If it finds a key that equals the one you're inserting, it overwrites the value; otherwise it appends the new entry to the bucket. Originally collisions were handled with a linked list, but since Java 8, if a single bucket grows beyond eight entries, it converts that list into a red-black tree, which keeps the worst case at log-n instead of linear. There's also resizing. HashMap has a load factor, default zero point seven five, and a capacity, default sixteen. Once the number of entries exceeds capacity times load factor — so twelve for the defaults — it doubles the capacity and rehashes all the existing entries into the bigger array. The get path mirrors the put path: it hashes the key the same way to find the bucket, then uses equals to find the exact entry within that bucket. This is exactly why both hashCode and equals matter — hashCode gets you to the right bucket, and equals identifies the right key inside it. If I had to summarize the whole thing: hash to a bucket, resolve collisions with a list or tree, use equals to match the key, and resize at the load factor threshold.

questions.question: What is the difference between HashMap, Hashtable, and ConcurrentHashMap?
questions.title: HashMap vs Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap
questions.direct_answer: **HashMap** is unsynchronized (fast, single-threaded), allows one null key/null values. **Hashtable** is a legacy class synchronized on every method (slow, no nulls). **ConcurrentHashMap** is the modern thread-safe map using fine-grained locking/CAS so reads are lock-free and writes lock only a segment — far more scalable than Hashtable, but no nulls. For concurrency, use ConcurrentHashMap, never Hashtable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the thread-safety and performance trade-offs and the modern recommendation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Recommending Hashtable for thread safety, or thinking Collections.synchronizedMap equals ConcurrentHashMap
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain ConcurrentHashMap's lock-free reads and segment/bin-level write locking vs Hashtable's whole-map lock

sections.title: Single-Threaded, Legacy, and Modern Concurrent
sections.content:
All three are **key-value maps** — you store a value under a key and fetch it back. The difference is **thread safety** and **performance**.

**`HashMap`** is unsynchronized. It is the fastest choice for single-threaded code, and it allows one null key and null values. The catch: it is not safe to share across threads.

**`Hashtable`** is a legacy class from before the Collections framework. Every method is `synchronized` on the **whole map**, so only one thread can touch it at a time. That makes it slow, and it forbids nulls.

**`ConcurrentHashMap`** is the modern thread-safe map. Reads are essentially **lock-free**, and a write locks only a small portion (a bin) using fine-grained locking and **CAS** (compare-and-swap). Many threads work at once, so it scales far better than Hashtable. It also forbids nulls.

> **The rule:** single-threaded -> `HashMap`; concurrent -> `ConcurrentHashMap`; `Hashtable` is obsolete.

sections.title: HashMap vs Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap
sections.content:
| Aspect | HashMap | Hashtable | ConcurrentHashMap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Thread-safe | No | Yes (whole-map lock) | Yes (fine-grained) |
| Performance | Fastest (1 thread) | Slow | Scales with threads |
| Null key/value | 1 null key, null values | None | None |
| Locking | none | every method | bin-level + CAS, lock-free reads |
| Iterator | fail-fast | fail-fast (enumerator) | weakly consistent |
| Status | current | legacy | current (concurrent) |

sections.title: Which Map for Which Job
sections.content:
emerald|HashMap|~Single-threaded default|unsynchronized, fastest|one null key, null values|not safe to share
rose|Hashtable|~Legacy, avoid|synchronized whole map|no nulls|serializes all access
blue|ConcurrentHashMap|~Concurrent choice|lock-free reads|bin-level write locks|no nulls, scales
amber|Rule of thumb|~Pick by threads|alone -> HashMap|shared -> ConcurrentHashMap|never Hashtable

sections.title: Wrong: HashMap shared across threads, or legacy Hashtable
Right: ConcurrentHashMap for concurrency
When to Use Each
sections.content: Use **HashMap** for all single-threaded or externally-synchronized code — it's the default. Use **ConcurrentHashMap** whenever multiple threads read and write the same map: caches, counters, shared lookups; prefer its atomic helpers (`merge`, `computeIfAbsent`). **Hashtable** has no modern use — it survives only for backward compatibility. Note `Collections.synchronizedMap` wraps a HashMap with a single lock (like Hashtable) and is still less scalable than ConcurrentHashMap.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Recommending `Hashtable` for thread safety.** It works, but the whole-map lock makes it a bottleneck — use `ConcurrentHashMap`.
- **Treating `Collections.synchronizedMap` as equal.** It wraps a single lock, so it serializes access just like Hashtable.
- **Putting nulls in the concurrent maps.** Both `Hashtable` and `ConcurrentHashMap` reject null keys and values.
- **Sharing a plain `HashMap`.** Concurrent writes can corrupt it or, in old JDKs, even spin forever.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **HashMap** — unsynchronized, fastest, one null key + null values; single-threaded.
- **Hashtable** — legacy, whole-map `synchronized`, no nulls; avoid.
- **ConcurrentHashMap** — fine-grained locking + lock-free reads, no nulls; the concurrent choice.
- ConcurrentHashMap scales with threads; Hashtable serializes all access.
- Use atomic methods: `merge`, `computeIfAbsent`, `compute`.
- `Collections.synchronizedMap` = single lock, less scalable than ConcurrentHashMap.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: All three are key-value maps, and the differences come down to thread safety and performance. HashMap is unsynchronized, so it's the fastest option for single-threaded code, and it allows one null key and null values. The catch is that it is not safe to share across threads — concurrent modification can corrupt it. Hashtable is the old legacy class from before the collections framework. It is thread-safe, but it achieves that by synchronizing every single method on the entire map, so only one thread can touch it at a time. That makes it a bottleneck, and it doesn't allow null keys or values. ConcurrentHashMap is the modern thread-safe map and the one you should actually reach for. Its reads are essentially lock-free, and its writes only lock a small portion of the map — a single bin or bucket — using fine-grained locking and compare-and-swap. So many threads can read and write concurrently without contending on one big lock, and it scales much better than Hashtable. Like Hashtable, it doesn't allow nulls, partly so that a get returning null unambiguously means absent. So the rule of thumb is simple: for single-threaded code use HashMap, for concurrent code use ConcurrentHashMap, and treat Hashtable as obsolete. One more thing worth mentioning: Collections.synchronizedMap wraps a HashMap with a single lock, which behaves a lot like Hashtable and is still less scalable than ConcurrentHashMap, so it's not a substitute. And with ConcurrentHashMap, prefer its atomic helpers like merge and computeIfAbsent for safe updates.

questions.question: Can HashMap have null keys and null values?
questions.title: HashMap Null Keys/Values
questions.direct_answer: Yes — **HashMap** allows **one null key** (stored in bucket 0, since `null` has no `hashCode()`) and **any number of null values**. By contrast, **Hashtable** and **ConcurrentHashMap** forbid null keys and values entirely. To tell a null value apart from a missing key, use `containsKey()`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know HashMap's null rules and how they differ from Hashtable/ConcurrentHashMap
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying HashMap allows multiple null keys, or using get()==null to test key presence
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain ConcurrentHashMap bans null so get()==null is unambiguous in concurrent code

sections.title: One Null Key, Many Null Values
sections.content:
A **HashMap** lets you store a `null` key and `null` values — with one limit. It permits exactly **one null key** and **as many null values** as you like.

The single null key is a special case. Since `null` has no `hashCode()`, HashMap cannot hash it, so it places that entry in **bucket 0**. Putting a second entry with a null key just **overwrites** the first, because keys stay unique.

Null values have no such cap — you can map any number of keys to `null`.

This is where the map types differ. **Hashtable** and **ConcurrentHashMap** throw `NullPointerException` for null keys *or* values. ConcurrentHashMap bans null on purpose: in concurrent code, a `get()` returning null must mean 'absent'. If null values were allowed, that result would be ambiguous — absent or mapped to null — which is unsafe across threads.

> **Practical rule:** use `containsKey()` (not `get() == null`) to tell a null value apart from a missing key.

sections.title: Null Rules Across Map Types
sections.content:
emerald|HashMap|~Most permissive|one null key (bucket 0)|many null values|keys still unique
rose|Hashtable|~Legacy, strict|no null key|no null value|throws NullPointerException
rose|ConcurrentHashMap|~Concurrency-safe|no null key|no null value|keeps get() unambiguous
amber|Telling them apart|~null value vs missing|use containsKey()|not get() == null|getOrDefault helps too

sections.title: Null Behavior in Code
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'Multiple null keys.'** Only one — a second null-key put overwrites the first.
- **`get() == null` to test presence.** That can't tell 'absent' from 'value is null'. Use `containsKey()`.
- **Assuming ConcurrentHashMap allows null.** It doesn't, by design.
- **Putting null in a `TreeMap`.** A natural-ordered TreeMap throws on a null key (it must compare it).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- HashMap: **one null key** (bucket 0) and **many null values**.
- A second null-key `put` **overwrites** the first.
- **Hashtable** and **ConcurrentHashMap** forbid null keys and values (`NullPointerException`).
- ConcurrentHashMap bans null to keep `get()` unambiguous across threads.
- Use **`containsKey()`** (or `getOrDefault`) to distinguish null value vs missing key.
- A natural-ordered `TreeMap` also rejects null keys.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Yes, a HashMap can have null keys and null values, but with a limit. It allows exactly one null key and any number of null values. The single null key is handled as a special case, because null doesn't have a hashCode, so HashMap just stores it in bucket zero. And since keys are unique, if you put a second entry with a null key, it simply overwrites the first one. Null values, on the other hand, have no such limit — you can map as many keys as you want to null. This is one of the classic differences between the map types. Hashtable, which is the old legacy class, doesn't allow null keys or null values at all; it throws a NullPointerException. ConcurrentHashMap also forbids null keys and values, and the reason is interesting: in concurrent code, if get returns null, it has to mean the key is absent. If null values were allowed, a null result would be ambiguous — it could mean absent or mapped to null — and that ambiguity is unsafe across threads, so they banned null outright. One practical tip that interviewers like: with a HashMap, don't test whether a key exists by checking if get returns null, because that can't distinguish a missing key from a key that's genuinely mapped to null. Use containsKey instead, or getOrDefault if you want a fallback. And note that a TreeMap with natural ordering also rejects null keys, because it has to compare them to sort.

questions.question: What are initial capacity and load factor in HashMap, and how do you choose them?
questions.title: HashMap Capacity and Load Factor
questions.direct_answer: **Initial capacity** is the number of buckets the table starts with (default **16**). **Load factor** is how full it may get before resizing (default **0.75**). When `size > capacity x loadFactor`, the table **doubles** and rehashes. To avoid resizes when you know the size n, set initial capacity to about `n / 0.75 + 1` (or `n / 0.75` rounded up to a power of two).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the resize trigger and how to pre-size to avoid rehashing
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting initial capacity to exactly n (forgetting the 0.75 factor still triggers a resize)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain capacity is always a power of two and the 0.75 default balances space vs collision rate

sections.title: Capacity, Load Factor, and Resizing
sections.content:
**Initial capacity** is the size of the bucket array when the map is created — the default is **16**. **Load factor** is how full the map may get before it grows — the default is **0.75**. Those two numbers are the part most beginners already half-know.

The twist is what they do together. Capacity is always rounded up to a **power of two**, so HashMap can compute the bucket index with a fast bitmask instead of a modulo.

The map tracks a **threshold** = `capacity x loadFactor` (12 for the defaults). When `size` exceeds it, the table **resizes** to double the capacity and **rehashes** every entry into the larger array — an O(n) operation.

The 0.75 default is a deliberate balance: a lower load factor wastes memory but cuts collisions; a higher one saves memory but raises collisions.

> **Pre-sizing rule:** if you'll insert `n` entries, set the initial capacity to about `n / 0.75 + 1` so the map never resizes mid-load.

sections.title: Capacity and Load Factor
sections.content:
blue|Initial capacity|~Bucket count at start|default 16|always a power of two|fast index via bitmask
emerald|Load factor|~Fullness threshold|default 0.75|balances space vs collisions|lower = fewer collisions
amber|Resize trigger|~When to grow|size > capacity * loadFactor|double capacity|rehash all entries (O(n))
rose|Pre-sizing|~Avoid resizes|know n entries?|set cap ~ n / 0.75 + 1|skips repeated rehashing

sections.title: Pre-Sizing to Avoid Resizes
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Setting capacity to exactly `n`.** The 0.75 factor still triggers a resize at `0.75 x n`; use `n / 0.75 + 1`.
- **Forgetting power-of-two rounding.** Capacity is always rounded up to a power of two internally.
- **Tuning the load factor blindly.** 0.75 is a good default; change it only with a measured reason.
- **Ignoring resize cost.** Each resize is O(n) and rehashes everything — wasteful in tight loops.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Initial capacity** = starting bucket count (default 16, power of two).
- **Load factor** = fullness threshold (default 0.75).
- Resize when **`size > capacity x loadFactor`**: double + rehash (O(n)).
- Pre-size with `new HashMap<>(n / 0.75 + 1)` to avoid resizes for n entries.
- Lower load factor = fewer collisions, more memory; higher = the reverse.
- Capacity is always rounded up to a **power of two**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Initial capacity is the number of buckets the HashMap starts with, and the default is sixteen. Internally it's always rounded up to a power of two, because that lets HashMap compute the bucket index with a fast bitmask instead of a modulo. Load factor is the threshold for how full the map can get before it grows, and the default is zero point seven five. HashMap keeps a threshold value equal to capacity times load factor — so twelve for the defaults — and when the number of entries exceeds that threshold, it resizes by doubling the capacity and rehashing every existing entry into the bigger array. That rehash is an O(n) operation, so you want to avoid doing it repeatedly. The zero point seven five default is a deliberate trade-off: a lower load factor means fewer collisions but wastes memory, while a higher one saves memory but increases collisions and slows lookups. For choosing them, the main practical lever is pre-sizing. If you know roughly how many entries you'll insert — say a thousand — don't set the initial capacity to exactly a thousand, because the load factor would still trigger a resize at seven hundred fifty. Instead set it to about n divided by zero point seven five, plus one, so roughly thirteen hundred, which gives enough room to hold all your entries without a single resize. The classic mistake interviewers look for is exactly that: setting capacity to n and forgetting the load factor still forces a resize. I'd generally leave the load factor at the default and only tune it if profiling showed a real reason.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of HashMap get() and put() operations?
questions.title: HashMap Time Complexity
questions.direct_answer: **get()** and **put()** are **O(1) on average** — the hash maps the key to a bucket directly. The worst case is **O(n)** if many keys collide into one bucket; since Java 8, a bucket that grows past 8 entries **treeifies** into a red-black tree, bounding the worst case at **O(log n)**. Good `hashCode()` distribution keeps you at O(1).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know average vs worst case and the Java 8 treeification improvement
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying HashMap is always O(1) with no mention of collisions or worst case
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain treeification (bucket -> red-black tree at 8 entries) caps worst case at O(log n)

sections.title: Average O(1), Worst Case Bounded
sections.content:
**`get()`** and **`put()`** on a HashMap are **O(1) on average** — constant time, no matter how big the map gets. That is the headline most beginners already know.

The reason is direct addressing. The key's `hashCode()` is spread (Java mixes the high bits down) and reduced to a bucket index, so the map jumps straight to the right bucket without scanning.

The nuance is the worst case. If many keys hash to the same bucket — say a `hashCode()` that returns a constant — that bucket becomes a long chain you must walk, which is **O(n)**.

Java 8 added a safeguard. Once a single bucket holds more than **8 entries** (and the table is large enough), it **treeifies** that bucket from a linked list into a **red-black tree**, so even a pathological bucket is **O(log n)** instead of O(n).

> **In practice:** with a well-distributed `hashCode()` and a sensible load factor, you stay at O(1).

sections.title: HashMap Complexity Cases
sections.content:
emerald|Average case|~O(1)|hash -> bucket directly|good hashCode spread|no scanning
rose|Worst case (legacy)|~O(n)|all keys one bucket|long linked-list chain|bad hashCode
blue|Java 8 treeify|~O(log n)|bucket > 8 entries|list becomes red-black tree|caps the worst case
amber|Keep it O(1)|~Best practice|strong hashCode|reasonable load factor|pre-size large maps

sections.title: Why It's O(1) on Average
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'Always O(1).'** It's *average* O(1); collisions can degrade it.
- **Ignoring treeification.** The Java 8 worst case is O(log n), not O(n).
- **Bad `hashCode()`.** Returning a constant funnels all keys into one bucket — worst-case behavior.
- **Confusing lookup with iteration.** Iterating the whole map is O(n + capacity), not O(1).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- `get()`/`put()` are **O(1) on average** via direct bucket addressing.
- **Worst case O(n)** when many keys collide into one bucket.
- **Java 8 treeification**: a bucket past 8 entries becomes a red-black tree -> **O(log n)**.
- A strong, well-distributed `hashCode()` keeps you at O(1).
- Iterating the whole map is **O(n + capacity)**.
- Resizing is an occasional O(n) cost; appends are amortized O(1).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: On average, both get and put on a HashMap are constant time, O(1). The reason is that HashMap uses the key's hashCode, spreads it out, and reduces it to a bucket index, so it can jump straight to the bucket where the entry lives without scanning anything. That's the whole point of a hash map. But it's important to qualify that with the worst case. If many keys hash to the same bucket — for example if you have a terrible hashCode that returns a constant — then that bucket turns into a long chain, and you have to walk it, which is linear time, O(n). Java 8 added an important improvement here. Once a single bucket grows beyond eight entries, and the table is large enough, HashMap converts that bucket from a linked list into a red-black tree. So even a badly behaved bucket is now O(log n) instead of O(n). That treeification caps the worst case. In practice, as long as you have a reasonable hashCode that distributes keys well and a sensible load factor, you stay at constant time. Two clarifications I'd add. First, don't just say HashMap is always O(1) — interviewers want to hear the average versus worst-case distinction and the treeification detail. Second, looking up a single key is O(1), but iterating the entire map is O(n plus capacity), because you walk every bucket. And resizing the table is an occasional O(n) operation, though appends are amortized constant time overall.

questions.question: Why must you override both equals() and hashCode() when using custom objects as HashMap keys?
questions.title: equals() and hashCode() Contract
questions.direct_answer: Because HashMap finds an entry in two steps: `hashCode()` picks the **bucket**, then `equals()` matches the **key** inside it. If you override only `equals()`, two equal objects may get different hash codes and land in different buckets, so lookups fail. The **contract**: equal objects MUST have equal hash codes — override both, using the same fields.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the two-step lookup and the equals/hashCode contract
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Overriding only equals() and being surprised that map.get(key) returns null for an equal object
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State the contract precisely: equal objects must have equal hashes; unequal objects may share a hash (collision)

sections.title: Two-Step Lookup Needs Both Methods
sections.content:
HashMap finds a key in **two steps**: first it calls `hashCode()` to choose the **bucket**, then it calls `equals()` to find the **exact key** inside that bucket. That two-step lookup is the whole reason both methods matter.

The **contract** is short: *if two objects are equal by `equals()`, they MUST return the same `hashCode()`.* (The reverse isn't required — unequal objects may share a hash code; that's just a collision.)

Now picture overriding only `equals()`. Two 'equal' keys can produce different hash codes, land in **different buckets**, and the map looks in the wrong place — `get` returns null even though the key is logically there.

Override only `hashCode()` and the opposite happens: the keys reach the same bucket, but the default `equals()` compares identity and says they differ.

So you override **both**, computed from the **same fields**.

> **The rule worth memorizing:** equal objects must have equal hash codes. Use `Objects.hash(...)`/`Objects.equals(...)`, or a `record`, which generates both correctly.

sections.title: The equals / hashCode Contract
sections.content:
blue|Step 1: hashCode|~Pick the bucket|maps key to a bucket index|must be consistent|same fields as equals
emerald|Step 2: equals|~Match the key|compares within the bucket|finds the exact entry|same fields as hashCode
rose|Override equals only|~Broken lookups|equal keys, different hashes|land in different buckets|get returns null
amber|The contract|~The rule|equal objects -> equal hashes|unequal may share a hash (collision)|override both together

sections.title: Override equals() only — lookups silently fail
Override both, from the same fields — lookups work
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Overriding only `equals()`.** The most common bug — `get` returns null for an equal key.
- **Using different fields.** `hashCode()` and `equals()` must use the **same** fields.
- **Mutable keys.** If a key's fields change after insertion, its hash changes and it's lost in the map.
- **Hand-writing buggy hashCode.** Prefer `Objects.hash(...)` or a `record` to avoid mistakes.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Lookup is two steps: `hashCode()` -> bucket, `equals()` -> exact key.
- **Contract**: equal objects MUST have equal hash codes.
- Override **both**, using the **same fields**.
- Override only `equals()` -> equal keys scatter to different buckets -> `get` returns null.
- Avoid **mutable** keys; a changed field corrupts the lookup.
- Use `Objects.hash`/`Objects.equals` or a Java `record` to generate both.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: It comes down to how HashMap finds things, which is a two-step process. First it calls hashCode on the key to decide which bucket to look in. Then, inside that bucket, it calls equals to find the exact key among any that collided there. Because both steps are involved, both methods have to be overridden and they have to agree. The formal rule is the equals-hashCode contract: if two objects are equal according to equals, they must return the same hashCode. The reverse is not required — two unequal objects are allowed to share a hash code, that's just a collision and HashMap handles it. Now picture what happens if you override only equals. You create a key, put a value in, then create a second key that's logically equal and call get. Since you didn't override hashCode, the two keys use the default identity hash, so they almost certainly produce different hash codes, land in different buckets, and the map looks in the wrong bucket and returns null. Your equal key is effectively invisible. If you override only hashCode, they reach the same bucket, but the default equals compares object identity, so it still says they're different. So you must override both, and crucially, compute them from the same set of fields. The easiest, safest way is to use Objects.hash and Objects.equals, or even better, use a Java record, which generates a correct equals and hashCode for you automatically. One more warning: avoid mutable keys, because if a field used in the hash changes after you've inserted the key, its hash changes and you'll never find it again.
